lesson.title: When Derivatives Run in Reverse: Meeting the Inverse Trig Integrals
lesson.summary: Some integrals do not simplify to polynomials or ordinary trig functions at all, they simplify to inverse trig functions, and this chapter previews the three key patterns that come directly from derivatives you already know.
lesson.body:
Every derivative rule you learn can be read in reverse to produce an integral rule, and the inverse trig functions are a perfect example of why that matters. You already know that the derivative of arcsin(x) is 1/√(1-x²). Turn that statement around and it becomes an integration fact for free: the indefinite integral of 1/√(1-x²) dx is arcsin(x) + C. Nothing new is being invented here, you are simply using the definition of an indefinite integral, the family of all antiderivatives of a function, and applying it to a derivative you already trust.

This chapter is the roadmap for three integral patterns that all come from inverse trig derivatives: 1/√(1-x²) integrates to arcsin(x), 1/(1+x²) integrates to arctan(x), and 1/(x√(x²-1)) integrates to arcsec(x) (for x > 1). None of these integrands look like they should produce anything as clean as an inverse trig function. They contain square roots and rational expressions with no obvious antiderivative among polynomials, exponentials, or ordinary trig functions. That is exactly the signal to watch for: when you see 1 over the square root of a constant minus x squared, or 1 over a constant plus x squared, or 1 over x times the square root of x squared minus a constant, you are looking at an inverse trig integral in disguise.

The skill here is pattern recognition, not derivation. Just as you learned to recognize x^n and reach for the power rule in reverse, you now learn to recognize these three algebraic shapes and reach for the matching inverse trig antiderivative. The next three chapters each take one of these shapes and work through it in full detail, including more general versions with a constant a in place of 1, such as 1/√(a²-x²).

Here is a first taste using the arcsin pattern. Evaluate the definite integral of 1/√(1-x²) dx from x = 0 to x = 1/2. Since the antiderivative is arcsin(x) + C, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives arcsin(1/2) minus arcsin(0). Now arcsin(1/2) is the angle whose sine is 1/2, which is π/6 (30 degrees), and arcsin(0) = 0. So the integral equals π/6 minus 0, which is π/6, about 0.5236. You can check the setup by differentiating arcsin(x) directly: its derivative is 1/√(1-x²), exactly the integrand you started with, confirming the antiderivative was the right one to use.

This entire chapter rests on two ideas you already have in hand: the indefinite integral, which says every derivative rule has a matching antiderivative rule, and the derivative of arcsin, which supplies the very first of these three patterns. Keep both in mind as you move into the arcsin, arctan, and arcsec integrals individually.
